Neonates of Gloydius blomhoffii emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs at a relatively modest size, with a wet weight at birth of 5.9 grams [Wwb = 5.9 grams]. This initial mass is consistent with the values reported for other small-bodied crotaline vipers, reflecting a reproductive strategy that prioritizes high fecundity over large offspring size. While the wet weight at birth is modest, the snout-vent length at birth has been recorded as 22.5 centimeters [Lb = 22.5 centimeters], though total length measurements from the literature suggest a range of 22 to 35 centimeters, with a mean value of approximately 28 centimeters. This combination of a relatively slender body and low mass likely facilitates the neonatal ability to hunt small ectothermic prey soon after the yolk-sac resorption stage is concluded. The emergence event itself, known as eclosion, typically occurs after the embryo has fully absorbed the yolk-dependent nutrients provided within the cleidoic egg. The completion of this yolk absorption stage marks the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical trophic switch that initiates the juvenile growth phase.

This lengthy developmental period, equivalent to five months, is a characteristic feature of temperate pitvipers that experience pronounced seasonal variation in thermal regimes. The temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C] appears to be near the optimal thermal range for embryonic growth, as development at lower temperatures would likely extend this period substantially, whereas higher temperatures risk desiccation of the sensitive amniote egg. Understanding this relationship between temperature and incubation duration is essential for predicting population responses to climate change.
